question: Explain Bagging, Boosting and Random forest.
expected_answer: Bagging (Bootstrap Aggregating) creates multiple subsets by random sampling with replacement, trains independent models on each, and combines predictions by voting (classification) or averaging (regression). It reduces variance. Boosting trains models sequentially, where each new model focuses on errors of previous models. It reduces bias. Examples: AdaBoost, Gradient Boosting, XGBoost. Random Forest is a specific bagging algorithm that uses decision trees and adds feature randomness - at each split, only a random subset of features is considered. This additional randomness further reduces variance and decorrelates the trees.

In contrast, boosting is a sequential ensemble method where models are trained to fix the mistakes of prior ones. Random Forest creates an ensemble of decision trees, each trained on a bootstrap sample of the data.

question: Explain the multihead self and cross attention in the transformer architecture with comparison.
expected_answer: Self-attention allows each position in a sequence to attend to all other positions in the same sequence, computing attention weights using Query, Key, Value matrices. Cross-attention allows a position in one sequence (e.g., decoder) to attend to all positions in another sequence (e.g., encoder output). Multi-head attention runs multiple attention heads in parallel with different learned projections, allowing the model to attend to information from different representation subspaces. Comparison: self-attention uses Q,K,V from the same sequence; cross-attention derives Q from one sequence and K,V from another.

The input is transformed into Query, Key and Value vectors through linear projections. Scaled dot-product attention: multiply Q by K transpose, divide by root of dimension, softmax, then multiply by V. The difference is that Q is derived from the target sequence and K, V from the source sequence in cross-attention. Multi-head attention means we perform the attention computation multiple times in parallel with diferent projections. Each attention head uses its own learned set of weight matrices (Wq, Wk, Wv) to project the input differently. Having multiple heads lets the model capture different types of relationships and patterns simultaneously. Self-attention operates within a single sequence, while cross-attention operates between two different sequences

question: What is Gradient descent? Explain Batch, stochastic and mini batch gradient descent comparatively.
expected_answer: Gradient descent is an iterative optimization algorithm used to minimize the loss/cost function by updating model parameters in the direction of the negative gradient. The learning rate controls step size. Batch GD computes gradients using the entire dataset per update - stable but slow for large data. Stochastic GD (SGD) uses one random sample per update - fast but noisy convergence. Mini-batch GD uses a small subset (batch) per update - balances speed and stability, most commonly used in practice.
student_answer: Gradient descent is an optimization algorithm used in machine learning. It reduces the error by finding the minimum value of the cost function. The learning rate is a key hyperparameter - too large causes overshooting, too small causes slow convergence. In the batch approach, you compute the average gradient across the whole training set before updating. With SGD, you randomly pick one sample, compute the gradient, and update immediately. Mini-batch GD splits the dataset into small batches and updates after each batch. Processing the full dataset each time makes batch GD slow; SGD is fast but mini-batch balances speed and resource usage. The convergence path of batch GD is smooth, SGD is erratic with high variance, and mini-batch provides reasonably stable convergence. Practically speaking, mini-batch GD is what everyone uses for training neural networks.

question: Explain the architecture of HDFS, YARN and Map-Reduce in Hadoop.
expected_answer: HDFS (Hadoop Distributed File System): Master-slave architecture with NameNode (stores metadata, manages namespace) and DataNodes (store actual data blocks). Files split into blocks (default 128MB) replicated across DataNodes. YARN (Yet Another Resource Negotiator): ResourceManager (global resource scheduler), NodeManager (per-node agent managing containers), ApplicationMaster (per-application coordinator). YARN separates resource management from job scheduling. MapReduce: Programming model with Map phase (processes input key-value pairs to produce intermediate pairs) and Reduce phase (aggregates intermediate values by key). JobTracker and TaskTracker in MRv1, replaced by YARN in MRv2.
student_answer: HDFS follows master-slave architecture to distribute and store data across multiple nodes reliably. Additionally, the NameNode is the master server that manages the file system namespace and stores metadata about files and directories. Each DataNode in the cluster stores data blocks locally and reports to the NameNode. Additionally, block-level storage with replication factor of 3 ensures data durability even when nodes fail. YARN is the resource management framework that separates resource management from data processing. Similarly, resourceManager is the central authority for resources, NodeManager manages resources on each individual node. Each application has its own ApplicationMaster that coordinates the execution of the application within the cluster. Next, the MapReduce framework processes data in parallel across the cluster using Map and Reduce functions. In the Reduce phase, all intermediate values for a given key are aggregated together to produce the output.

question: Explain the methods of Reducing overfitting in deep learning models shortly.
expected_answer: Overfitting occurs when a model learns noise in training data and performs poorly on unseen data. Key methods to reduce it: (1) Dropout - randomly deactivates neurons during training to prevent co-adaptation. (2) Regularization (L1/L2) - adds penalty term to loss function to constrain weights. (3) Data augmentation - increases training data variety through transformations. (4) Early stopping - halts training when validation loss starts increasing. (5) Batch normalization - normalizes layer inputs, has regularizing effect. (6) Reducing model complexity - using fewer layers/neurons. (7) Cross-validation for model selection.
student_answer: When a model overfits, it learns the training data too well, capturing noise rather than the underlying pattern. L1 and L2 regularization add a penalty term to the loss function based on the magnitude of weights, discouraging large weight values. Meanwhile, by applying random transformations to training images (flip, rotate, zoom), data augmentation increases dataset diversity. We use early stopping by tracking the validation loss and stopping training when it no longer decreases. Batch normalization helps with overfitting to some extent because of the noise it introduces during mini-batch processing. Also, reducing model complexity by using fewer layers or neurons helps prevent overfitting. Getting more data is the simplest and often most effective way to address overfitting. On the other hand, we use a validation set or cross-validation to tune hyperparameters and detect overfitting early.

question: Explain Bagging, Boosting and Random forest.

Meanwhile, random Forest creates an ensemble of decision trees, each trained on a bootstrap sample of the data. It is also worth mentioning that random Forest adds feature randomness by considering only a random subset of features at each split point. Then, rF builds many decision trees on bootstrapped subsets of the data and aggregates their predictions. Another point is that random Forest adds feature randomness by considering only a random subset of features at each split point. question: Explain the multihead self and cross attention in the transformer architecture with comparison.
expected_answer: Self-attention allows each position in a sequence to attend to all other positions in the same sequence, computing attention weights using Query, Key, Value matrices. Cross-attention allows a position in one sequence (e.g., decoder) to attend to all positions in another sequence (e.g., encoder output). Multi-head attention runs multiple attention heads in parallel with different learned projections, allowing the model to attend to information from different representation subspaces. Comparison: self-attention uses Q,K,V from the same sequence; cross-attention derives Q from one sequence and K,V from another.
student_answer: Well, q, K, V are computed from the input embeddings. Q represents what we're looking for, K represents what we have, and V represents the actual content. In cross-attention, the attention is computed between two separate sequences rather than within one sequence. Different projection matrices per head mean each head can specialize in capturing different patterns. The attention weights are calculated by taking the dot product of Q and K, dividing by the square root of the dimension, applying softmax, then multiplying by V. Multi-head attention runs several attention operations in parallel, each called a head. In self-attention, every token in the input sequence computes attention weights with respect to all other tokens in the same sequence. The difference is that Q is derived from the target sequence and K, V from the source sequence in cross-attention. Each head can focus on different aspects of the input - some on local patterns, some on long-range dependencies.

By using cross-validation, we can choose the model complexity that generalizes best to unseen data. Overfitting means the model has low training error and low test error. question: What is Batch Normalisation? Write the 5 assumptions of linear regression.
expected_answer: Batch Normalization normalizes the input of each layer by adjusting and scaling activations using mini-batch statistics (mean and variance). It reduces internal covariate shift, speeds up training, and allows higher learning rates. During inference, it uses running averages. Five assumptions of linear regression: (1) Linearity - relationship between X and Y is linear. (2) Independence - observations are independent. (3) Homoscedasticity - constant variance of errors. (4) Normality - residuals are normally distributed. (5) No multicollinearity - independent variables are not highly correlated.
student_answer: As far as I know, the five assumptions are: linearity, independence of errors, homoscedasticity, normality of residuals, and no multicollinearity. The assumption of no multicollinearity means the features should be independent of each other. The spread of the residuals should be roughly the same across all predicted values. At inference time, the running mean and running variance stored during trainning are used for normalization. Independence assumption means the error terms are not correlated with each other. BN speeds up training by allowing higher learning rates and reducing the sensitivity to initialization. After normalization, batch norm applies a learned scale (gamma) and shift (beta) to restore the representation power. Batch Normalization is a technique that normalizes layer inputs by adjusting them to have zero mean and unit variance using batch statistics. The relationship between features and target must be linear.

question: Explain Bagging, Boosting and Random forest.
expected_answer: Bagging (Bootstrap Aggregating) creates multiple subsets by random sampling with replacement, trains independent models on each, and combines predictions by voting (classification) or averaging (regression). It reduces variance. Boosting trains models sequentially, where each new model focuses on errors of previous models. It reduces bias. Examples: AdaBoost, Gradient Boosting, XGBoost. Random Forest is a specific bagging algorithm that uses decision trees and adds feature randomness - at each split, only a random subset of features is considered. This additional randomness further reduces variance and decorrelates the trees.

question: Explain the architecture of HDFS, YARN and Map-Reduce in Hadoop.
expected_answer: HDFS (Hadoop Distributed File System): Master-slave architecture with NameNode (stores metadata, manages namespace) and DataNodes (store actual data blocks). Files split into blocks (default 128MB) replicated across DataNodes. YARN (Yet Another Resource Negotiator): ResourceManager (global resource scheduler), NodeManager (per-node agent managing containers), ApplicationMaster (per-application coordinator). YARN separates resource management from job scheduling. MapReduce: Programming model with Map phase (processes input key-value pairs to produce intermediate pairs) and Reduce phase (aggregates intermediate values by key). JobTracker and TaskTracker in MRv1, replaced by YARN in MRv2.
student_answer: Hadoop MapReduce is a computational model that divides work into Map and Reduce steps for distributed processing. The Map phase aggregates results and the Reduce phase splits data. DataNodes are the workers that store the actual data and serve read/write requests.

question: Explain the multihead self and cross attention in the transformer architecture with comparison.
expected_answer: Self-attention allows each position in a sequence to attend to all other positions in the same sequence, computing attention weights using Query, Key, Value matrices. Cross-attention allows a position in one sequence (e.g., decoder) to attend to all positions in another sequence (e.g., encoder output). Multi-head attention runs multiple attention heads in parallel with different learned projections, allowing the model to attend to information from different representation subspaces. Comparison: self-attention uses Q,K,V from the same sequence; cross-attention derives Q from one sequence and K,V from another.
student_answer: Self-attention lets each word look at every other word in the same sentence to understand context. Attention scores are computed as softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d_k)) * V, where d_k is the key dimension for scaling.

question: Explain the methods of Reducing overfitting in deep learning models shortly.
expected_answer: Overfitting occurs when a model learns noise in training data and performs poorly on unseen data. Key methods to reduce it: (1) Dropout - randomly deactivates neurons during training to prevent co-adaptation. (2) Regularization (L1/L2) - adds penalty term to loss function to constrain weights. (3) Data augmentation - increases training data variety through transformations. (4) Early stopping - halts training when validation loss starts increasing. (5) Batch normalization - normalizes layer inputs, has regularizing effect. (6) Reducing model complexity - using fewer layers/neurons. (7) Cross-validation for model selection.
student_answer: With early stopping, we halt training at the point where the validation error starts to rise. Regularization like L2 (Ridge) adds the sum of squared wieghts to the loss, and L1 (Lasso) adds absolute values, constraining model complexity.
